description:
I’m a Biomedical Engineering student from Mexico, passionate about healthcare technology, programming, electronics, robotics, and space exploration. I’m particularly interested in developing innovative solutions that combine biomedical engineering and software to improve human health. I bring a multidisciplinary perspective, problem-solving skills, and a strong willingness to learn and collaborate.

I’m looking for teammates with skills in software development.
summary: ByteMedicals is an integrated web platform that lets astronauts assess their own health during long-duration missions and act on it. It brings together, in a single system, vital-sign monitoring (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, oxygen saturation, pain and weight), cumulative radiation, 17 NASA medical condition categories, an interactive 3D anatomical figure, and an AI assistant with memory that answers from the knowledge-base documents and cites its sources. It addresses the challenge from NASA's Human Research Program five hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and closed and hostile environments. It matters because on a mission to Mars the crew will be up to 20 minutes away in communications and years away from a hospital: early self-assessment, symptom logging and trend monitoring can make the difference between acting in time or not. All values shown are simulated and labelled as such; the platform never diagnoses or prescribes.
details: What it does. A health dashboard with green, yellow and red alerts; Vital Signs with a dedicated chart for each of the 7 signs; cumulative radiation against NASA's career limit (~600 mSv); Frequent Conditions with NASA's 17 categories, each with its own chart and acquisition levels (continuous, periodic, clinical); an interactive 3D anatomical figure by body system; a Health Log with symptom logging and 6 original self-check questionnaires; Medications; Spaceflight Hazards; Risk Assessment; and an AI assistant that remembers conversations, tracks symptom evolution and answers with the current mission context. How it works. The browser talks to a Python backend (FastAPI, port 8000), which authenticates with JWT, stores users and conversations in MySQL, and forwards questions to PRAG (port 8001), the AI engine that queries Qdrant and Ollama (qwen2.5:3b-instruct model) over the documents synced from Google Drive, citing its sources. Telemetry is simulated and deterministic, with its provenance labelled (simulated, manual or real). Benefits. One platform instead of several separate apps; self-assessment in plain language; symptom memory across conversations; and a record for the crew medical officer. What I hope to achieve. That an astronaut can assess their health, log how they feel, watch trends and know when to raise the alarm, without depending on Earth. Tools. Python, FastAPI, JavaScript, Three.js, HTML/CSS, MySQL, Qdrant, Ollama, LangChain and the Google Drive API.
